documentTitle: Matcha On Ice Cafe — Equipment & Bar Manual

sections.label: The Grinder
sections.blurb: Fiorenzato E64 Evo Pro — 64mm flat burrs, on-demand dosing, stepless adjustment.

story.heading: Fiorenzato E64 Evo Pro
body: The E64 Evo Pro is a 64mm flat-burr commercial grinder built for on-demand dosing — it grinds fresh for each shot rather than sitting pre-ground in a hopper, dosed through a programmable touchscreen rather than a mechanical doser.

Grind size is set with a stepless micrometric adjustment collar, so there's no click-stops to count. Dial in gradually and taste — or better, time the shot — rather than chasing a specific number on the collar.

callout.label: Grind Adjustment
callout.note: There's no "correct number" — only what lands the shot in the 25–30 sec window from Espresso Basics. Adjust in small increments and re-taste.

sections.label: The Espresso Machine
sections.blurb: Sanremo Zoe Compact, 2 group — independent PID-controlled boilers per group.

story.heading: Sanremo Zoe Compact
body: The Zoe Compact is a 2-group machine with independently PID-controlled boilers per group — each side can be dialed to its own brew temperature, useful for running more than one bean on the bar at once.

Temperature stability depends on a full warm-up before service. A machine that's merely "on" isn't necessarily ready — give the boilers and group heads time to stabilize before pulling shots for guests.

callout.label: Warm-Up Time
callout.note: Pull and discard a couple of shots once warm to confirm both groups are stable and matched.

sections.label: Steaming Milk
sections.blurb: Stretch, then texture — the two stages behind velvety microfoam.

story.heading: Microfoam
body: Good microfoam is glossy and velvety, with no visible bubbles — thick enough to hold latte art, light enough to integrate into the drink rather than sitting on top like dry foam.

It's built in two stages, the same logic as Cold Foam: first stretch, incorporating air near the surface while the milk is still cool and the volume grows; then texture, submerging the wand to spin that air into the milk until it's smooth.

callout.label: Target Temperature
callout.note: Stop just before this range — residual heat carries it the rest of the way. Past 170°F / 77°C, milk scalds and turns sweet-flat.

method: Purge the wand briefly to clear condensation before steaming.
Submerge the tip just below the surface, slightly off-center, to begin stretching — a light hissing or tearing sound means air is incorporating.
Once the volume has grown by about a third, submerge the tip fully and angle it to create a whirlpool, texturing out any large bubbles.
Keep spinning the milk until the pitcher is warm to the touch and near the target temperature.
Purge and wipe the wand immediately after every use.
Tap the pitcher on the counter and swirl to pop any remaining bubbles before pouring.

sections.label: Barista Tools
sections.blurb: The kit on the bar — what each piece is for, and how to keep it that way.

drinks.name: Tamper
method: Distribute the grounds evenly before tamping.
Tamp level and firm, straight down — consistent pressure, not forced.
drinks.note: An off-level tamp is one of the most common causes of channeling.

drinks.name: WDT Tool
method: Stir through the dose in a circular motion after grinding, before tamping.
Break up any clumps and redistribute the grounds evenly across the basket.
drinks.note: Especially useful on darker roasts, which clump more from surface oils.

drinks.name: Digital Scale
method: Weigh the dose before grinding.
Weigh the shot as it pulls, to hit the target yield.
drinks.note: Dose, yield and time together — not the clock alone — is what makes a shot repeatable.

drinks.name: Milk Pitchers
method: Match the pitcher to the drink — a smaller pour is easier to control in a smaller pitcher.
Fill no more than halfway before steaming, to leave room for the milk to expand.
drinks.note: Rinse immediately after each use — dried milk is the hardest to get out.

drinks.name: Knock Box
method: Knock the spent puck out of the portafilter with a firm, single motion.
Empty and rinse it out through service, not just at close.
drinks.note: A full knock box slows everyone down — empty it before it's overflowing.

drinks.name: Puck Screen
method: Place on top of the dose before tamping.
Wipe clean between shots; it keeps the group head cleaner and reduces channeling.
drinks.note: Not a substitute for a good distribution and tamp — it just keeps the mess contained.

drinks.name: Cleaning Kit
method: Backflush at the intervals set out in The Espresso Machine's Startup & Care.
Brush the group head daily; deep-clean the shower screen and gasket weekly.
drinks.note: A clean group head is a taste issue before it's a hygiene one — old coffee oils turn rancid fast.
